quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: Don't let the spelling of "lawn" guide you — isolate the exact consonant sound and test it against both options.
quests.explanation: Once you isolate the consonant in "lawn", it's clearly /n/ — produced by touching your tongue tip to the ridge behind your top teeth and letting the sound hum out through your nose. Words with /ŋ/ instead, like "sing", require raising the back of your tongue to the soft palate and letting the sound hum out through your nose.
quests.mouthPosition: Touch your tongue tip to the ridge behind your top teeth and let the sound hum out through your nose.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: For /d/, the trick is to tap your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth with your voice on — like the start of "day". Check whether "dose" really does that.
quests.explanation: /d/ is the sound in "dose", formed by tapping your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth with your voice on. Learners often mix this up with /ð/, a voiced dental fricative made by placing your tongue tip lightly behind your top teeth and blowing with your voice on, but the mouth is doing something different each time.
quests.mouthPosition: To produce this sound, tap your tongue tip on the ridge behind your top teeth with your voice on.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE TARGET CONSONANT PHONEME IN THE WORD
quests.hint: "use" needs careful listening. A voiced palatal approximant like /j/ can sound close to a voiced postalveolar affricate like /dʒ/ if you're not paying attention to exactly what your mouth is doing.
quests.explanation: This is /j/, not /dʒ/: in "use", you raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth and glide, like starting to say "ee". The distractor would instead need stopping the air just behind your top teeth, then releasing it as a hiss, with your voice on, which changes the sound completely.
quests.mouthPosition: Feel it in the mouth: raise the middle of your tongue toward the roof of your mouth and glide, like starting to say "ee".
